claim: TMCO1 can be natively isolated in association with ribosome-Sec61 complexes.
source: consistent with a role in a co-translational process at the ER membrane, it can be natively isolated in association with ribosome-Sec61 complexes (Anghel et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Anghel et al., 2017)

claim: Ribosomal proteins, subunits of the Sec61 complex, and TMCO1 were enriched in affinity purification from 3xFlag-TMCO1 HEK293 cells relative to control cells.
source: Ribosomal proteins, subunits of the Sec61 complex, and TMCO1 were enriched relative to control cells lacking the Flag tag

claim: Known translocon accessory factors including OST, TRAP, TRAM, Sec62/63 and signal peptidase complex were either weakly enriched or absent in TMCO1 affinity purification.
source: whereas known translocon accessory factors—including subunits of the OST and TRAP complexes, TRAM, Sec62/63 and the signal peptidase complex—were either weakly enriched or absent.

claim: CCDC47, Nicalin, and two subunits of the Nicalin-TMEM147-NOMO complex were strongly enriched in TMCO1 affinity purification.

claim: The catalytic OST subunit STT3A was not detected in TMCO1-ribosome complexes.
source: Notably, the catalytic OST subunit STT3A was not detected, consistent with the absence of OST from the TMCO1-ribosome complexes.

claim: Affinity purification via a Flag tag on Nicalin recovered TMCO1, CCDC47 and NOMO in the ribosome-bound fraction.

claim: TMCO1, CCDC47 and the Nicalin-TMEM147-NOMO complex can be isolated as a single, ribosome-associated complex.
source: indicating that these proteins can be isolated as a single, ribosome-associated complex.

claim: In the absence of ribosomes, only components of the Nicalin-TMEM147-NOMO complex remained intact.
source: In the absence of ribosomes, however, only components of the Nicalin-TMEM147-NOMO complex remained intact (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B showing immunoprecipitation from ribosome-free fractions

claim: TMCO1, CCDC47 and the pre-formed Nicalin-TMEM147-NOMO complex assemble in the context of the ribosome.
source: suggesting that TMCO1, CCDC47 and the pre-formed Nicalin-TMEM147-NOMO complex assemble in the context of the ribosome.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that these components only co-purify in the presence of ribosomes

claim: CCDC47, Nicalin, TMEM147 and NOMO are abundant ER-localized proteins, conserved across eukaryotes.
source: CCDC47, Nicalin, TMEM147 and NOMO are abundant ER-localized proteins, conserved across eukaryotes, widely expressed in human tissues, and associated with several human diseases (Itzhak et al., 2016; Burdon et al., 2011; Sharma et al., 2012; Xin et al., 2010; Caglayan et al., 2013; Alanay et al., 2014; Li et al., 2019; Reuter et al., 2017; Morimoto et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: CCDC47, Nicalin, TMEM147 and NOMO are widely expressed in human tissues and associated with several human diseases.
source: CCDC47, Nicalin, TMEM147 and NOMO are abundant ER-localized proteins, conserved across eukaryotes, widely expressed in human tissues, and associated with several human diseases (Itzhak et al., 2016; Burdon et al., 2011; Sharma et al., 2012; Xin et al., 2010; Caglayan et al., 2013; Alanay et al., 2014; Li et al., 2019; Reuter et al., 2017; Morimoto et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: CCDC47 has been linked to various membrane-associated processes.
source: CCDC47 has been linked to various membrane-associated processes (Morimoto et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2007; Konno et al., 2012; Thapa et al., 2018; Yamamoto et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: The Nicalin-TMEM147-NOMO complex has been proposed to regulate subunit assembly and localization of several cell surface receptors and ion channels.
source: the Nicalin-TMEM147-NOMO complex has been proposed to regulate subunit assembly and localization of several cell surface receptors and ion channels (Almedom et al., 2009; Gottschalk et al., 2005; Kamat et al., 2014; Rosemond et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: TMCO1, CCDC47, Nicalin and NOMO were identified in a genome-wide screen for factors that impair surface expression of a mutant TRP channel.
source: More recently, all four genes were identified in a genome-wide screen for factors that impair surface expression of a mutant TRP channel (Talbot et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: The stable isolation of CCDC47, Nicalin, TMEM147 and NOMO with TMCO1-bound ribosome-Sec61 complexes suggests a link to a co-translational process at the ER.
source: That these proteins can be stably isolated with TMCO1-bound ribosome-Sec61 complexes suggests a link between these observations and a co-translational process at the ER.
evidence: Inferred from the biochemical isolation data and previous functional studies

claim: 1229 unique, high-confidence intra- and inter-protein cross-links were identified in the affinity-purified TMCO1 complexes by XL-MS.
source: Using chemical cross-linking and mass spectrometry (XL-MS), we identified 1229 unique, high-confidence intra- and inter-protein cross-links in the affinity-purified complexes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by cross-linking mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Multiple cross-links between 60S ribosomal subunits and the cytosolic-facing regions of Sec61, TMCO1, CCDC47, TMEM147 and NOMO confirmed their predicted membrane topologies.
source: Multiple cross-links between 60S ribosomal subunits and the cytosolic-facing regions of Sec61, TMCO1, CCDC47, TMEM147 and NOMO confirmed their predicted membrane topologies
evidence: Supported by cross-linking mass spectrometry data

claim: Cross-links between 60S ribosomal subunits and Sec61, TMCO1, CCDC47, TMEM147 and NOMO placed them in the vicinity of the ribosome exit tunnel.
source: Multiple cross-links between 60S ribosomal subunits and the cytosolic-facing regions of Sec61, TMCO1, CCDC47, TMEM147 and NOMO confirmed their predicted membrane topologies, and placed them in the vicinity of the ribosome exit tunnel (Figure 1D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by cross-linking mass spectrometry data

claim: The cryo-EM structure of natively purified TMCO1 complexes reveals hybrid state A/P and P/E tRNAs.
source: Density for the ribosome is well-defined, revealing hybrid state A/P and P/E tRNAs, and a mixture of nascent polypeptides in the exit tunnel (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM density map shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A

claim: The cryo-EM structure reveals a mixture of nascent polypeptides in the ribosome exit tunnel.
source: Density for the ribosome is well-defined, revealing hybrid state A/P and P/E tRNAs, and a mixture of nascent polypeptides in the exit tunnel (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM density map

claim: Local resolution within the translocon varies from ~3.5–4.5 Å in Sec61 and regions contacting the ribosome.
source: Local resolution within the translocon varies from ~3.5–4.5 Å in Sec61 and regions contacting the ribosome, to ~5.5–7.5 Å for most of the membrane region, and ~10–15 Å in peripheral and luminal regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and Figure 2—figure supplement 5B,C).
evidence: Supported by local resolution analysis of cryo-EM maps

claim: Sec61 is in a conformation with a closed lateral gate and the plug helix occluding the central pore.
source: Sec61 is in a conformation similar to that observed in the ribosome-Sec61-OST complex (Braunger et al., 2018), with a closed lateral gate and the plug helix occluding the central pore (Figure 2—figure supplement 5D).
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM structure and comparison to previous structure

claim: A cluster of eight TMDs visible near the Sec61 hinge were assigned to the Nicalin-TMEM147 sub-complex using a homology model based on the APH1-Nicastrin sub-complex of human γ-secretase.
source: A cluster of eight TMDs visible near the Sec61 hinge were unambiguously assigned to the Nicalin-TMEM147 sub-complex using a homology model based on the APH1-Nicastrin sub-complex of human γ-secretase (Figure 2—figure supplement 6; Dettmer et al., 2010; Bai et al., 2015; Haffner et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM density fitting with homology model and citations to previous structural and functional studies

claim: The distinctive arrangement of the seven TMEM147 TMDs could be docked into the density as a rigid body with only minor adjustments.
source: The distinctive arrangement of the seven TMEM147 TMDs could be docked into the density as a rigid body with only minor adjustments (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 5E).
evidence: Supported by model building into cryo-EM density

evidence: Supported by cryo-EM density map shown in Figure 2D

claim: The cytosolic end of TM3 in TMEM147 is ten residues shorter than the corresponding TM3 in APH-1.
source: Notably, the cytosolic end of TM3 in TMEM147 is ten residues shorter than the corresponding TM3 in APH-1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 6E).
evidence: Supported by sequence and structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6E

claim: The shorter TM3 in TMEM147 allows it to bind Sec61 despite limited space in the ribosome-translocon junction.
source: This allows TMEM147 to bind Sec61 despite limited space in the ribosome-translocon junction
evidence: Inferred from structural analysis comparing TMEM147 to APH-1

claim: The short cytosolic regions of TMEM147 are positioned in contact with uL24 and rRNA H7, in agreement with XL-MS data.
source: and positions the short cytosolic regions of TMEM147 in contact with uL24 and rRNA H7, in agreement with the XL-MS (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).

claim: A cluster of three TMDs adjacent to the Nicalin-TMEM147 sub-complex were assigned to TMCO1.
source: Adjacent to the Nicalin-TMEM147 sub-complex is a cluster of three TMDs, which were assigned to TMCO1 (Figure 2E).

source: We generated a model of TMCO1 using RaptorX-Contact (Wang et al., 2017; Xu, 2019), which employs co-evolutionary data and deep learning for distance-based structure prediction (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling method and citations

claim: The RaptorX-Contact model of TMCO1 recapitulates the conserved three TMD core, N-out/C-in topology, and cytosolic-facing coiled-coil found in members of the Oxa1 superfamily.
source: The model recapitulates the conserved three TMD core, N-out/C-in topology, and cytosolic-facing coiled-coil found in members of the Oxa1 superfamily (Anghel et al., 2017; Borowska et al., 2015; Kumazaki et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by computational model and citations to previous structural studies

claim: The TMCO1 model could be placed into cryo-EM density with only minor adjustments.
source: and could be placed into density with only minor adjustments.
evidence: Supported by model building into cryo-EM density

claim: The conserved and positively charged coiled-coil of TMCO1 extends out of the membrane into the cytosolic vestibule where it packs against rRNA H19, H24 and uL24.
source: The conserved and positively charged coiled-coil of TMCO1 extends out of the membrane into the cytosolic vestibule where it packs against a surface on the ribosome that includes rRNA H19, H24 and uL24.
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM structure

claim: The ribosome-binding mode of TMCO1 agrees with the proposed ribosome-binding mode of bacterial YidC.
source: This agrees with the proposed ribosome-binding mode of bacterial YidC (Kedrov et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by comparison to previous study on YidC

claim: The TMCO1 structure satisfies numerous inter- and intra-molecular cross-links observed by XL-MS.
source: satisfies numerous inter- and intra-molecular cross-links observed by XL-MS (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D)
evidence: Supported by agreement between cryo-EM structure and cross-linking data

claim: The TMCO1 structure rationalizes the previously reported ribosome-binding activity of TMCO1.
source: and rationalizes the previously reported ribosome-binding activity of TMCO1 (Anghel et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis and citation to previous functional study

claim: A globular density in the cytosolic vestibule curls out of the membrane near TMCO1 and terminates in a long helical extension that traces along the ribosome surface.
source: The most prominent feature in the cytosolic vestibule is a globular density that curls out of the membrane near TMCO1 and terminates in a long helical extension that traces along the ribosome surface (Figure 2F).

claim: A model of the large cytosolic region of CCDC47 was generated using RaptorX-Contact, revealing a long and flexible C-terminal coiled-coil extending from a globular N-terminal domain.
source: Using RaptorX-Contact we generated a model of the large cytosolic region of CCDC47, revealing a long and flexible C-terminal coiled-coil extending from a globular N-terminal domain (Figure 2—figure supplement 8).

claim: The globular domain of CCDC47 contacts eL6 and rRNA H25.
source: The globular domain of CCDC47 contacts eL6 and rRNA H25

source: The translocon extends ~90 x 120 x 140 Å

source: with Sec61 and its accessory factors arranged near the ribosome exit tunnel and significant mass on both sides of the membrane (Figure 3A).

source: Ribosome binding is mediated by multiple protein-protein and protein-RNA contacts (Figure 3A,C).

source: These position the cytosolic domains of TMCO1 and CCDC47 near the nascent chain as it emerges from the ribosome exit tunnel

claim: The luminal Nicalin domain is placed near translocated segments of the nascent chain.
source: and place the luminal Nicalin domain near translocated segments of the nascent chain.

source: In bacterial YidC, this funnel operates as a transient binding site for TMDs, which are then released into the membrane (Kumazaki et al., 2014; Borowska et al., 2015).

claim: TMCO1 is located on the 'back' side of Sec61 in the TMCO1 translocon.
source: TMCO1 is located on the 'back' side of Sec61 in the TMCO1 translocon (Figure 4B).

claim: The TMCO1 funnel lines the lipid-filled cavity at the center of the translocon.
source: Here, the TMCO1 funnel lines the lipid-filled cavity at the center of the translocon

claim: The seven TMDs of TMEM147 form a funnel that extends from the lumen partway across the membrane.
source: TMEM147 also lines the lipid-filled cavity. Here, its seven TMDs form a funnel that extends from the lumen partway across the membrane.

source: Within the bilayer, the Sec61 hinge (located between TM5 and TM6) contacts TM2, TM3 and TM4 inside the TMEM147 funnel.

claim: The Sec61 hinge only partially occupies the TMEM147 funnel, laterally sealing it in membrane, but leaving it open to the lumen.

claim: The TMEM147 funnel arrangement is reminiscent of the Hrd1 protein conducting ERAD channel, which has a hydrophilic funnel that opens to the cytosol and is laterally sealed by a neighboring Hrd1 subunit.
source: This is reminiscent of the Hrd1 protein conducting ERAD channel, in which a structurally similar hydrophilic funnel, proposed to transport transmembrane segments from the bilayer to the cytosol, opens to the cytosol, and is laterally sealed by a neighboring Hrd1 subunit (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C; Schoebel et al., 2017).

claim: TMEM147 could insert a hydrophobic segment from the lumen into the central membrane cavity in a process gated by Sec61.

claim: The structural observations suggest that the TMCO1 translocon may be specialized for membrane protein biogenesis.
source: Taken together, these structural observations suggest that the TMCO1 translocon may be specialized for membrane protein biogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from structural features including the funnels and central cavity

claim: RIP-seq analysis showed strong enrichment for transcripts encoding secretory pathway transmembrane proteins in TMCO1-associated ribosomes.
source: Remarkably, we observed strong enrichment for transcripts encoding secretory pathway transmembrane proteins (Figure 5A).

claim: Single-pass membrane proteins were strongly depleted in TMCO1-associated ribosomes.
source: Of these, single-pass proteins—by far the most abundant type of membrane protein in the human genome—were strongly depleted (Figure 5B).

claim: Transcripts encoding multi-pass membrane proteins with four or more TMDs were enriched in TMCO1-associated ribosomes.
source: By contrast, transcripts encoding multi-pass membrane proteins with four or more TMDs were enriched (Figure 5B).

source: These include numerous transporters, receptors, transferases and hydrolases (Figure 5C).

claim: Enrichment of TMCO1-linked transcripts was observed across three orders of magnitude of transcript abundance in the input sample.
source: Consistent with selective enrichment of TMCO1-linked transcripts, we observed enrichment across three orders of magnitude of transcript abundance in the input sample (Figure 5D)

claim: Transcript enrichment in TMCO1-associated ribosomes was independent of protein length.
source: and this was independent of protein length (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: RIP-seq data directly link the TMCO1 translocon to a co-translational process involving hundreds of different multi-pass clients.
source: These data directly link the TMCO1 translocon to a co-translational process involving hundreds of different multi-pass clients.

claim: The steady-state expression level of EAAT1 was reduced by ~3 fold in TMCO1 knockout cells compared to wild-type cells.

source: Similar reductions were observed in Nicalin (2.4-fold), TMCO1/Nicalin (2.8-fold) and TMCO1/CCDC47 (3.8-fold) single- and double-knockout cells
evidence: Supported by western blot quantification data

claim: EAAT1 expression was reduced by 3.8-fold in TMCO1/CCDC47 double knockout cells.
source: Similar reductions were observed in Nicalin (2.4-fold), TMCO1/Nicalin (2.8-fold) and TMCO1/CCDC47 (3.8-fold) single- and double-knockout cells
evidence: Supported by western blot quantification data

claim: A single CCDC47 knockout showed only a modest 1.6-fold reduction in EAAT1 expression.
source: while a single CCDC47 (1.6-fold) knockout showed only a modest reduction (Figure 5F,G).

claim: The steady-state expression levels and glycosylation patterns of two single-pass membrane proteins, integrin α5 and TRAPα, were unchanged in TMCO1 knockout cells.

evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: TMCO1 disruption does not lead to a general defect in membrane protein biogenesis.
source: demonstrating that TMCO1 disruption does not lead to a general defect in membrane protein biogenesis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Little change in EAAT1 mRNA levels was observed in TMCO1, Nicalin and CCDC47 single- and double-knockout cells.

source: Together with the structural analysis, these data implicate the TMCO1 translocon in multi-pass membrane protein biogenesis.

claim: TMCO1, CCDC47 and the Nicalin-TMEM147-NOMO complex are conserved components of an ER translocon that functions co-translationally with Sec61 during biogenesis of multi-pass membrane proteins.

claim: The TMCO1 translocon functions as an insertase and intramembrane chaperone.
source: Although we do not formally exclude a role in client-specific targeting to the ER, we propose that the TMCO1 translocon functions as an insertase and intramembrane chaperone.

claim: The structural model for TMCO1 is consistent with its evolutionary relationship to members of the Oxa1 superfamily, including YidC, Get1, EMC3 and Ylp1.
source: Our structural model for TMCO1 is consistent with its evolutionary relationship to members of the Oxa1 superfamily, including YidC, Get1, EMC3 and Ylp1 (Anghel et al., 2017).

claim: Members of the Oxa1 superfamily have evolved to function in different contexts, but their ability to move transmembrane segments into the membrane appears to be conserved.

claim: Hydrophobic segments of the nascent chain that inefficiently engage with Sec61 could access the membrane through the conserved cytosolic TMCO1 funnel.

claim: Hydrophobic segments that have translocated across the bilayer through the canonical Sec61 channel might access the membrane through the luminal TMEM147 funnel.

claim: As segments integrate, the central cavity of the translocon could shield the nascent chain to minimize misfolding and degradation.
source: As segments integrate, the central cavity of the translocon could shield the nascent chain to minimize misfolding and degradation.
evidence: Proposed function based on structural features

claim: Organizing putative insertion and shielding functions in a single translocon might increase the efficiency with which different biophysical and topological features of the nascent chain are accommodated during multi-pass membrane protein biogenesis.
source: Organizing these putative functions in a single translocon might increase the efficiency with which different biophysical and topological features of the nascent chain are accommodated during multi-pass membrane protein biogenesis (Cymer et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2000; Skach, 2009).
evidence: Proposed functional advantage based on structural organization and citations to previous work on membrane protein biogenesis challenges

claim: The translocon is a dynamic assembly whose subunit composition varies temporally to meet the demands of a particular client.

evidence: Supported by the data presented and citations to previous work

claim: TMCO1, CCDC47 and the Nicalin-TMEM147-NOMO complex are abundant proteins.
source: TMCO1, CCDC47 and the Nicalin-TMEM147-NOMO complex are abundant (Itzhak et al., 2016)
